**Cooks Monument and Reserve** is a heritage-listed [memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial "Memorial") at Charlotte Street, [Cooktown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooktown,_Queensland "Cooktown, Queensland"), [Shire of Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shire_of_Cook "Shire of Cook"), [Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland "Queensland"), Australia. It was designed in the office of the [Queensland Colonial Architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Colonial_Architect "Queensland Colonial Architect") and built by Hobbs and Carter in 1887. It was added to the [Queensland Heritage Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Heritage_Register "Queensland Heritage Register") on 30 April 1997.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Captain_Cook_Memorial%2C_Cooktown.jpg/250px-Captain_Cook_Memorial%2C_Cooktown.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Captain_Cook_Memorial,_Cooktown.jpg)

Original design of the monument included a statue of Cook at the top

The Cook Monument at Cooktown was erected in 1887 by Hobbs and Carter of [South Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Brisbane,_Queensland "South Brisbane, Queensland"), to designs prepared in the office of the Queensland Colonial Architect, [George St Paul Connolly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_St_Paul_Connolly?action=edit&redlink=1 "George St Paul Connolly (page does not exist)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

Cooktown had been established in September 1873 as the [Endeavour River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endeavour_River "Endeavour River") port for the [Palmer River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmer_River "Palmer River") goldfields. By the mid-1880s it was serving one of the most significant goldfields in Queensland. A railway was constructed from Cooktown to [Laura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura,_Queensland "Laura, Queensland") between 1884 and 1888, further opening the port to development. By the late 1880s Cooktown had become the important centre not only of a thriving mining district (boosted by the 1887 discovery of tin along the [Annan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annan_River "Annan River")), but also of [pearling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_diving "Pearl diving"), [beche-de-mer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_cucumber_as_food "Sea cucumber as food"), and pastoral activity. After 1885, Cooktown was also the main port for Queensland trade with [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea "New Guinea").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

In May 1886, the then [Premier of Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Queensland "Premier of Queensland"), Sir [Samuel Walker Griffith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Walker_Griffith "Samuel Walker Griffith"), travelled to Cooktown and other northern ports on a tour of inspection, partly associated with defence issues, more with political strategy. The [Separation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_North_Queensland?action=edit&redlink=1 "Separation of North Queensland (page does not exist)") movement was gaining momentum in [Townsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Townsville "Townsville") and the far north, and Griffith was keen to demonstrate his government's commitment to, and concern for, northern Queensland. The [Cooktown Municipal Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooktown_Municipal_Council "Cooktown Municipal Council") at this time was seeking to commemorate [James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook")'s encampment at the Endeavour River in the winter of [1770](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1770,_Queensland "1770, Queensland"), and it appears that Griffith, as political expediency, committed the Colonial Architect's office to designing the Cook monument at Cooktown.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

The Cooktown Municipal Council had intended that the monument include a statue of James Cook, but when tenders were called in June 1886, then again in September 1886 and February 1887 with different materials specified, they were for the column only. In December 1887 Sir Samuel Griffith re-visited Cooktown, and when requested by the mayor to provide assistance in commissioning the statue, refused, stating that it was more important to commemorate the event than the person.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

The contract had been let in February 1887 to Hobbs and Carter of South Brisbane, with a price of [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_pound "Australian pound")1,059 and completion time of 8 months. It appears that the memorial was not constructed on the site originally proposed, which necessitated an additional foundation, bringing the final cost to [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_pound "Australian pound")1,297. The foundation stone was laid on 1 September 1887 by the Mayor of Cooktown, John Savage, and the work had been completed by January 1888. [Sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone") used in the construction came from [Murphys Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murphys_Creek,_Queensland "Murphys Creek, Queensland") in southeast Queensland, and it was reputedly the first stone structure erected in Cooktown.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

Around the monument, a small (1.5 acres (0.61 ha)) reserve for municipal purposes was gazetted in June 1888. A brick-lined town well, believed to have been built by the Cooktown Municipal Council to service ships berthed at the nearby Cooktown wharves, was constructed in the reserve, south of the monument. This work probably was undertaken post-1888, as the Council filled in much of the Cook Monument Reserve in 1889. A small vertical boiler engine pumped water from the well to the wharves through a 3" diameter pipe. It is understood that the well has also supplied adjacent Charlotte Street businesses from time to time.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

In the 20th century, several other memorials were erected within the reserve:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

*   Kennedy Memorial: a granite cairn erected in 1948 to honour British explorer [Edmund Besley Court Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Besley_Court_Kennedy "Edmund Besley Court Kennedy"), who was killed by Aborigines on [Cape York Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_York_Peninsula "Cape York Peninsula") (part of Cook Shire) in December 1848. Kennedy's exploratory work helped to open [far north Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_North_Queensland "Far North Queensland") to pastoral settlement in the mid-19th century. The memorial was unveiled on 25 September 1948 by the Chair of the [Cook Shire Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shire_of_Cook "Shire of Cook"), Mayor WCH Hodges.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)
*   National Horse Trail Marker: a small granite cairn erected in August 1977 to mark the beginning of the [National Horse Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Horse_Trail "The National Horse Trail") from Cooktown to Melbourne, and the epic ride of Dan Seymour, who in the early 1970s demonstrated the feasibility of such a trail. The trail was mapped between 1974 and the 1980s, when it was made a bi-centennial project. Sections are used regularly, but few people have ridden the full distance. The marker was erected by the Australian Trail Horse Riders' Association and was unveiled by Henry Tranter, President of the Tablelands Trail Horse Riders' Club.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)
*   Annan River Water Supply Memorial Fountain: in 1989 the old town well on the reserve was cleaned out and a fountain constructed over it to commemorate the inauguration in November 1989 of a new permanent water supply from the [Annan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annan_River "Annan River") to Cooktown. The Annan River pipeline was a joint federal, state and local government project, replacing Cooktown's previous water supply from the bore fields on the southern outskirts of the town.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)
*   1803 Cannon: There is now located in the reserve a cannon cast in 1803 in [Carron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carron,_Falkirk "Carron, Falkirk"), Scotland, and bearing the royal monogram GR. During the height of the "Russian invasion" scare of 1885, the Cooktown Municipal Council telegraphed to the [Premier of Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Queensland "Premier of Queensland"), requesting him to supply arms, ammunition and an officer to take charge of the Cooktown volunteer defence force. This cannon was sent, along with 3 cannonballs, 2 rifles and 1 officer. Initially the cannon was located on the foreshore near the [Cooktown Powder Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooktown_Powder_Magazine "Cooktown Powder Magazine") on Webber Esplanade, overlooking the entrance to Cooktown Harbour on the Endeavour River estuary. It is fired once a year as part of the annual Cook's landing re-enactment celebrations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Description")]

Cook's Monument is situated in a small reserve located between Charlotte Street and the Endeavour River estuary, on a slight rise adjacent to the site where James Cook beached the barque Endeavour for repairs in mid-1770. The reserve is grassed, with palms and mature trees around the perimeter.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

The monument comprises a tall, slender sandstone [column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Column "Column"), topped with a detailed capital, which rises from a square [pedestal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedestal "Pedestal") resting upon a granite base and [plinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plinth "Plinth"). The steps of the plinth lead to a square dado incorporating drinking [fountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fountain "Fountain") on each side. These fountains were once linked to a regular water supply [possibly an internal tank], and the water outlets emerge from the mouths of sculpted animal heads. The dado is set beneath a modest [entablature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entablature "Entablature") and the [pediment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pediment "Pediment") is flanked by sandstone urns at each corner.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

To the north of the Cook Monument is the 1803 cannon sent in 1885 to Cooktown by the Queensland colonial government, for the use of the local volunteer defence force. It stands on a concrete platform. Adjacent to the gun is an interpretative sign.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

To the south of the Cook Monument, but within the same reserve, are three more recent memorials and the early town well:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

*   Kennedy Memorial: a conical-shaped granite cairn, approximately 1.2 metres (3 ft 11 in) high, resting on a concrete base, with an embossed brass plaque in the face addressing Charlotte Street.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)
*   National Horse Trail Marker: a simple granite cairn or marker approximately 0.5 metres (1 ft 8 in) high, conical in shape, with an embossed brass plaque in the face addressing Charlotte Street.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)
*   Annan River Water Supply Memorial Fountain and Early Town Well: The fountain comprises a series of metal water pipes constructed over an early, brick-lined town well. The well has a diameter of 23 feet (7.0 m) at ground level, from which the shaft is bricked down 16 feet (4.9 m) to a 4-foot-6-inch (1.37 m) wide ledge, after which it narrows to 14-foot (4.3 m) diameter, and is bricked down a further 8 feet 4 inches (2.54 m), at the bottom of which are granite slabs. In the wall of the upper shaft are two arched entrances, now filled in with rubble, leading to underground spider channels or aqueducts which formerly fed the well with storm water run-off, in addition to the ground water from below. Formerly there were three cross-logs let into the walls near the top, for roof joist supports. Adjacent to the well was a tank stand with engine and boiler beneath. Water was pumped form the well to the tank, then from the tank to the wharves via a galvanised pipe along the foreshore. .Above the bricks are several courses of cement blocks [added at a later date], topped by a metal railing added in 1989 as part of the conversion to a fountain. The capacity of the well is approximately 47,000 imperial gallons (210,000 L; 56,000 US gal).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

## Heritage listing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Heritage listing")]

Cooks Monument and Reserve was listed on the [Queensland Heritage Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Heritage_Register "Queensland Heritage Register") on 30 April 1997 having satisfied the following criteria.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

**The place is important in demonstrating the evolution or pattern of Queensland's history.**

Cook's Monument and Reserve is significant historically for its commemoration of Cook's encampment below Grassy Hill, at the mouth of the Endeavour River, in mid-1770 - the first official British sojourn on the east coast of Australia. The place is significant also as Queensland's earliest memorial to James Cook and the crew of the Endeavour, and illustrates Cooktown's early developed sense of historical importance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

The site contains an early brick-lined town well, which is important in illustrating the establishment of municipal services in early Cooktown.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

**The place is important in demonstrating the principal characteristics of a particular class of cultural places.**

The monument is a fine example of its type and one of the finest sandstone public memorials in Queensland. It is also an excellent example of the work of the Queensland colonial architect's office under George St Paul Connolly.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

**The place is important because of its aesthetic significance.**

Its aesthetic setting within a grassy, treed reserve contributes significantly to the townscape of Cooktown, and from the Endeavour River estuary is a Cooktown landmark.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

**The place has a strong or special association with a particular community or cultural group for social, cultural or spiritual reasons.**

The place has a special association for the people of Cooktown with their sense of historical identity. A number of other memorials have been placed in the reserve, illustrating this continued association.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

**Cooks Monument and Reserve** is a heritage-listed [memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial "Memorial") at Charlotte Street, [Cooktown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooktown,_Queensland "Cooktown, Queensland"), [Shire of Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shire_of_Cook "Shire of Cook"), [Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland "Queensland"), Australia. It was designed in the office of the [Queensland Colonial Architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Colonial_Architect "Queensland Colonial Architect") and built by Hobbs and Carter in 1887. It was added to the [Queensland Heritage Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Heritage_Register "Queensland Heritage Register") on 30 April 1997.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Captain_Cook_Memorial%2C_Cooktown.jpg/250px-Captain_Cook_Memorial%2C_Cooktown.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Captain_Cook_Memorial,_Cooktown.jpg)

Original design of the monument included a statue of Cook at the top

The Cook Monument at Cooktown was erected in 1887 by Hobbs and Carter of [South Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Brisbane,_Queensland "South Brisbane, Queensland"), to designs prepared in the office of the Queensland Colonial Architect, [George St Paul Connolly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_St_Paul_Connolly?action=edit&redlink=1 "George St Paul Connolly (page does not exist)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

Cooktown had been established in September 1873 as the [Endeavour River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endeavour_River "Endeavour River") port for the [Palmer River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmer_River "Palmer River") goldfields. By the mid-1880s it was serving one of the most significant goldfields in Queensland. A railway was constructed from Cooktown to [Laura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura,_Queensland "Laura, Queensland") between 1884 and 1888, further opening the port to development. By the late 1880s Cooktown had become the important centre not only of a thriving mining district (boosted by the 1887 discovery of tin along the [Annan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annan_River "Annan River")), but also of [pearling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_diving "Pearl diving"), [beche-de-mer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_cucumber_as_food "Sea cucumber as food"), and pastoral activity. After 1885, Cooktown was also the main port for Queensland trade with [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea "New Guinea").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

In May 1886, the then [Premier of Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Queensland "Premier of Queensland"), Sir [Samuel Walker Griffith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Walker_Griffith "Samuel Walker Griffith"), travelled to Cooktown and other northern ports on a tour of inspection, partly associated with defence issues, more with political strategy. The [Separation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_North_Queensland?action=edit&redlink=1 "Separation of North Queensland (page does not exist)") movement was gaining momentum in [Townsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Townsville "Townsville") and the far north, and Griffith was keen to demonstrate his government's commitment to, and concern for, northern Queensland. The [Cooktown Municipal Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooktown_Municipal_Council "Cooktown Municipal Council") at this time was seeking to commemorate [James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook")'s encampment at the Endeavour River in the winter of [1770](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1770,_Queensland "1770, Queensland"), and it appears that Griffith, as political expediency, committed the Colonial Architect's office to designing the Cook monument at Cooktown.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

The Cooktown Municipal Council had intended that the monument include a statue of James Cook, but when tenders were called in June 1886, then again in September 1886 and February 1887 with different materials specified, they were for the column only. In December 1887 Sir Samuel Griffith re-visited Cooktown, and when requested by the mayor to provide assistance in commissioning the statue, refused, stating that it was more important to commemorate the event than the person.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

The contract had been let in February 1887 to Hobbs and Carter of South Brisbane, with a price of [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_pound "Australian pound")1,059 and completion time of 8 months. It appears that the memorial was not constructed on the site originally proposed, which necessitated an additional foundation, bringing the final cost to [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_pound "Australian pound")1,297. The foundation stone was laid on 1 September 1887 by the Mayor of Cooktown, John Savage, and the work had been completed by January 1888. [Sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone") used in the construction came from [Murphys Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murphys_Creek,_Queensland "Murphys Creek, Queensland") in southeast Queensland, and it was reputedly the first stone structure erected in Cooktown.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

Around the monument, a small (1.5 acres (0.61 ha)) reserve for municipal purposes was gazetted in June 1888. A brick-lined town well, believed to have been built by the Cooktown Municipal Council to service ships berthed at the nearby Cooktown wharves, was constructed in the reserve, south of the monument. This work probably was undertaken post-1888, as the Council filled in much of the Cook Monument Reserve in 1889. A small vertical boiler engine pumped water from the well to the wharves through a 3" diameter pipe. It is understood that the well has also supplied adjacent Charlotte Street businesses from time to time.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

In the 20th century, several other memorials were erected within the reserve:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

*   Kennedy Memorial: a granite cairn erected in 1948 to honour British explorer [Edmund Besley Court Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Besley_Court_Kennedy "Edmund Besley Court Kennedy"), who was killed by Aborigines on [Cape York Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_York_Peninsula "Cape York Peninsula") (part of Cook Shire) in December 1848. Kennedy's exploratory work helped to open [far north Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_North_Queensland "Far North Queensland") to pastoral settlement in the mid-19th century. The memorial was unveiled on 25 September 1948 by the Chair of the [Cook Shire Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shire_of_Cook "Shire of Cook"), Mayor WCH Hodges.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)
*   National Horse Trail Marker: a small granite cairn erected in August 1977 to mark the beginning of the [National Horse Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Horse_Trail "The National Horse Trail") from Cooktown to Melbourne, and the epic ride of Dan Seymour, who in the early 1970s demonstrated the feasibility of such a trail. The trail was mapped between 1974 and the 1980s, when it was made a bi-centennial project. Sections are used regularly, but few people have ridden the full distance. The marker was erected by the Australian Trail Horse Riders' Association and was unveiled by Henry Tranter, President of the Tablelands Trail Horse Riders' Club.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)
*   Annan River Water Supply Memorial Fountain: in 1989 the old town well on the reserve was cleaned out and a fountain constructed over it to commemorate the inauguration in November 1989 of a new permanent water supply from the [Annan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annan_River "Annan River") to Cooktown. The Annan River pipeline was a joint federal, state and local government project, replacing Cooktown's previous water supply from the bore fields on the southern outskirts of the town.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)
*   1803 Cannon: There is now located in the reserve a cannon cast in 1803 in [Carron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carron,_Falkirk "Carron, Falkirk"), Scotland, and bearing the royal monogram GR. During the height of the "Russian invasion" scare of 1885, the Cooktown Municipal Council telegraphed to the [Premier of Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Queensland "Premier of Queensland"), requesting him to supply arms, ammunition and an officer to take charge of the Cooktown volunteer defence force. This cannon was sent, along with 3 cannonballs, 2 rifles and 1 officer. Initially the cannon was located on the foreshore near the [Cooktown Powder Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooktown_Powder_Magazine "Cooktown Powder Magazine") on Webber Esplanade, overlooking the entrance to Cooktown Harbour on the Endeavour River estuary. It is fired once a year as part of the annual Cook's landing re-enactment celebrations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Description")]

Cook's Monument is situated in a small reserve located between Charlotte Street and the Endeavour River estuary, on a slight rise adjacent to the site where James Cook beached the barque Endeavour for repairs in mid-1770. The reserve is grassed, with palms and mature trees around the perimeter.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

The monument comprises a tall, slender sandstone [column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Column "Column"), topped with a detailed capital, which rises from a square [pedestal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedestal "Pedestal") resting upon a granite base and [plinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plinth "Plinth"). The steps of the plinth lead to a square dado incorporating drinking [fountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fountain "Fountain") on each side. These fountains were once linked to a regular water supply [possibly an internal tank], and the water outlets emerge from the mouths of sculpted animal heads. The dado is set beneath a modest [entablature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entablature "Entablature") and the [pediment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pediment "Pediment") is flanked by sandstone urns at each corner.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

To the north of the Cook Monument is the 1803 cannon sent in 1885 to Cooktown by the Queensland colonial government, for the use of the local volunteer defence force. It stands on a concrete platform. Adjacent to the gun is an interpretative sign.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

To the south of the Cook Monument, but within the same reserve, are three more recent memorials and the early town well:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

*   Kennedy Memorial: a conical-shaped granite cairn, approximately 1.2 metres (3 ft 11 in) high, resting on a concrete base, with an embossed brass plaque in the face addressing Charlotte Street.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)
*   National Horse Trail Marker: a simple granite cairn or marker approximately 0.5 metres (1 ft 8 in) high, conical in shape, with an embossed brass plaque in the face addressing Charlotte Street.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)
*   Annan River Water Supply Memorial Fountain and Early Town Well: The fountain comprises a series of metal water pipes constructed over an early, brick-lined town well. The well has a diameter of 23 feet (7.0 m) at ground level, from which the shaft is bricked down 16 feet (4.9 m) to a 4-foot-6-inch (1.37 m) wide ledge, after which it narrows to 14-foot (4.3 m) diameter, and is bricked down a further 8 feet 4 inches (2.54 m), at the bottom of which are granite slabs. In the wall of the upper shaft are two arched entrances, now filled in with rubble, leading to underground spider channels or aqueducts which formerly fed the well with storm water run-off, in addition to the ground water from below. Formerly there were three cross-logs let into the walls near the top, for roof joist supports. Adjacent to the well was a tank stand with engine and boiler beneath. Water was pumped form the well to the tank, then from the tank to the wharves via a galvanised pipe along the foreshore. .Above the bricks are several courses of cement blocks [added at a later date], topped by a metal railing added in 1989 as part of the conversion to a fountain. The capacity of the well is approximately 47,000 imperial gallons (210,000 L; 56,000 US gal).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

## Heritage listing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Heritage listing")]

Cooks Monument and Reserve was listed on the [Queensland Heritage Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Heritage_Register "Queensland Heritage Register") on 30 April 1997 having satisfied the following criteria.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

**The place is important in demonstrating the evolution or pattern of Queensland's history.**

Cook's Monument and Reserve is significant historically for its commemoration of Cook's encampment below Grassy Hill, at the mouth of the Endeavour River, in mid-1770 - the first official British sojourn on the east coast of Australia. The place is significant also as Queensland's earliest memorial to James Cook and the crew of the Endeavour, and illustrates Cooktown's early developed sense of historical importance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

The site contains an early brick-lined town well, which is important in illustrating the establishment of municipal services in early Cooktown.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

**The place is important in demonstrating the principal characteristics of a particular class of cultural places.**

The monument is a fine example of its type and one of the finest sandstone public memorials in Queensland. It is also an excellent example of the work of the Queensland colonial architect's office under George St Paul Connolly.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

**The place is important because of its aesthetic significance.**

Its aesthetic setting within a grassy, treed reserve contributes significantly to the townscape of Cooktown, and from the Endeavour River estuary is a Cooktown landmark.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooks_Monument_and_Reserve#cite_note-qhr-1)

**The place has a strong or special association with a particular community or cultural group for social, cultural or spiritual reasons.**

The **Battle of Trocadero**, fought on 31 August 1823, was a significant battle in France's [expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Thousand_Sons_of_Saint_Louis "Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis") in support of the Spanish King [Ferdinand VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_VII "Ferdinand VII"). The French defeated the Spanish liberal forces and restored Ferdinand to absolute rule.

## Prelude

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Trocadero&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Prelude")]

After the downfall of [Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon "Napoleon"), King Ferdinand VII of Spain refused to adopt the liberal [Spanish Constitution of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Constitution_of_1812 "Spanish Constitution of 1812") and in 1820 faced a rebellion in favour of a [constitutional monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy "Constitutional monarchy"), led by [Rafael del Riego y Nuñez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_del_Riego_y_Nu%C3%B1ez "Rafael del Riego y Nuñez"). On March 10, 1820, in the Plaza de San Juan de Dios in [Cádiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1diz "Cádiz"), Royalist absolutist troops carried out a massacre against those of the population of Cádiz who supported the liberals and were celebrating the proclamation of the Constitution of 1812.

The King was captured and detained at Cádiz. Alarmed by these events, the other [European powers convened](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert_of_Europe "Concert of Europe") in October 1822 at the [Congress of Verona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_Verona "Congress of Verona") and authorized France to intervene in the conflict and restore the rule of Ferdinand, with only [Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland") abstaining from that decision.

## Military intervention

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Trocadero&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military intervention")]

[![Image 11](http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Cadiz_MKL_Bd._3_1890_%28128592667%29.jpg/250px-Cadiz_MKL_Bd._3_1890_%28128592667%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cadiz_MKL_Bd._3_1890_(128592667).jpg)

Location of Trocadero in the Bay of Cádiz (1890)

On 17 April 1823, French forces led by [Louis-Antoine, Duke of Angoulême](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis-Antoine,_Duke_of_Angoul%C3%AAme "Louis-Antoine, Duke of Angoulême"), son of the future [Charles X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_X_of_France "Charles X of France"), crossed the [Pyrenees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenees "Pyrenees") into Spain.

The French forces were welcomed by the [Basques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basques "Basques") and conservative Spaniards. The Duke dispatched a force to besiege [San Sebastián](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Sebasti%C3%A1n "San Sebastián") while he launched an attack on [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid"), held by the rebel government, which on 23 May withdrew to [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville"). Madrid's military commander secretly surrendered and fled to France, and the leaderless Madrid garrison could not keep out the French, who seized the city and installed a [regent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_de_Alc%C3%A1ntara_%C3%81lvarez_de_Toledo,_13th_Duke_of_the_Infantado "Pedro de Alcántara Álvarez de Toledo, 13th Duke of the Infantado"), pending Ferdinand's expected return.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Trocadero#cite_note-2)

The French moved south to deal with the rebels at Cádiz, and besieged the fort of [Trocadero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isla_del_Trocadero "Isla del Trocadero"), which controlled access to the city. On 31 August 1823 they launched a surprise bayonet attack from the sea side, taking advantage of the low tide, and took the fort. After this action, French infantry captured the Trocadero village by a flank attack. After this last action, 1700 Spanish soldiers were captured by the French.

Cádiz itself held out for three weeks despite bombardments, but was forced to surrender on 23 September 1823 and King Ferdinand was released and handed over to the French. Despite a prior promise of amnesty, the King ordered reprisals against the rebels; in the following years, an estimated 30,000 people were executed and 20,000 imprisoned.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 12](http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Duque_de_Angulema_en_el_Trocadero%3B_Hippolyte_Delaroche.jpg/250px-Duque_de_Angulema_en_el_Trocadero%3B_Hippolyte_Delaroche.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Duque_de_Angulema_en_el_Trocadero;_Hippolyte_Delaroche.jpg)

_[The Duke of Angoulême at the Taking of Trocadero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Duke\_of\_Angoul%C3%AAme\_at\_the\_Taking\_of\_Trocadero "The Duke of Angoulême at the Taking of Trocadero")_ by [Paul Delaroche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Delaroche "Paul Delaroche"), 1828

The Battle of Trocadero was one of the events that prompted U.S. President [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe") to proclaim what would become known as the [Monroe Doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monroe_Doctrine "Monroe Doctrine") on 2 December 1823, to safeguard the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas "Americas") against intervention by European powers.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Trocadero#cite_note-3)

The fall of Trocadero was commemorated in Paris, with the [Trocadéro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trocad%C3%A9ro,_Paris "Trocadéro, Paris"), where the city was expanding to the edges of the [Bois de Boulogne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bois_de_Boulogne "Bois de Boulogne"). [Louis-Antoine, Duke of Angoulême](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis-Antoine,_Duke_of_Angoul%C3%AAme "Louis-Antoine, Duke of Angoulême"), the victor of the battle, was offered the title "Prince of Trocadero" by the Spanish king, but he refused to accept it, partly in disgust at Ferdinand going back on his promises of clemency.

In _[Les Misérables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les\_Mis%C3%A9rables "Les Misérables")_, [Victor Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Hugo "Victor Hugo") devoted several paragraphs to the battle (Volume II, Book 2, chapter 3), in which he called the battle "a fine military action", but also said that "[t]he war of 1823 was an outrage on the generous Spanish nation, (..) at the same time, an outrage on the French Revolution."

The **Battle of Trocadero**, fought on 31 August 1823, was a significant battle in France's [expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Thousand_Sons_of_Saint_Louis "Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis") in support of the Spanish King [Ferdinand VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_VII "Ferdinand VII"). The French defeated the Spanish liberal forces and restored Ferdinand to absolute rule.

## Prelude

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Trocadero&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Prelude")]

After the downfall of [Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon "Napoleon"), King Ferdinand VII of Spain refused to adopt the liberal [Spanish Constitution of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Constitution_of_1812 "Spanish Constitution of 1812") and in 1820 faced a rebellion in favour of a [constitutional monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy "Constitutional monarchy"), led by [Rafael del Riego y Nuñez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_del_Riego_y_Nu%C3%B1ez "Rafael del Riego y Nuñez"). On March 10, 1820, in the Plaza de San Juan de Dios in [Cádiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1diz "Cádiz"), Royalist absolutist troops carried out a massacre against those of the population of Cádiz who supported the liberals and were celebrating the proclamation of the Constitution of 1812.

The King was captured and detained at Cádiz. Alarmed by these events, the other [European powers convened](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert_of_Europe "Concert of Europe") in October 1822 at the [Congress of Verona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_Verona "Congress of Verona") and authorized France to intervene in the conflict and restore the rule of Ferdinand, with only [Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland") abstaining from that decision.

## Military intervention

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Trocadero&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military intervention")]

[![Image 11](http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Cadiz_MKL_Bd._3_1890_%28128592667%29.jpg/250px-Cadiz_MKL_Bd._3_1890_%28128592667%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cadiz_MKL_Bd._3_1890_(128592667).jpg)

Location of Trocadero in the Bay of Cádiz (1890)

On 17 April 1823, French forces led by [Louis-Antoine, Duke of Angoulême](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis-Antoine,_Duke_of_Angoul%C3%AAme "Louis-Antoine, Duke of Angoulême"), son of the future [Charles X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_X_of_France "Charles X of France"), crossed the [Pyrenees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenees "Pyrenees") into Spain.

The French forces were welcomed by the [Basques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basques "Basques") and conservative Spaniards. The Duke dispatched a force to besiege [San Sebastián](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Sebasti%C3%A1n "San Sebastián") while he launched an attack on [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid"), held by the rebel government, which on 23 May withdrew to [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville"). Madrid's military commander secretly surrendered and fled to France, and the leaderless Madrid garrison could not keep out the French, who seized the city and installed a [regent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_de_Alc%C3%A1ntara_%C3%81lvarez_de_Toledo,_13th_Duke_of_the_Infantado "Pedro de Alcántara Álvarez de Toledo, 13th Duke of the Infantado"), pending Ferdinand's expected return.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Trocadero#cite_note-2)

The French moved south to deal with the rebels at Cádiz, and besieged the fort of [Trocadero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isla_del_Trocadero "Isla del Trocadero"), which controlled access to the city. On 31 August 1823 they launched a surprise bayonet attack from the sea side, taking advantage of the low tide, and took the fort. After this action, French infantry captured the Trocadero village by a flank attack. After this last action, 1700 Spanish soldiers were captured by the French.

Cádiz itself held out for three weeks despite bombardments, but was forced to surrender on 23 September 1823 and King Ferdinand was released and handed over to the French. Despite a prior promise of amnesty, the King ordered reprisals against the rebels; in the following years, an estimated 30,000 people were executed and 20,000 imprisoned.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Aftermath

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Trocadero&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Aftermath")]

[![Image 12](http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Duque_de_Angulema_en_el_Trocadero%3B_Hippolyte_Delaroche.jpg/250px-Duque_de_Angulema_en_el_Trocadero%3B_Hippolyte_Delaroche.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Duque_de_Angulema_en_el_Trocadero;_Hippolyte_Delaroche.jpg)

_[The Duke of Angoulême at the Taking of Trocadero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Duke\_of\_Angoul%C3%AAme\_at\_the\_Taking\_of\_Trocadero "The Duke of Angoulême at the Taking of Trocadero")_ by [Paul Delaroche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Delaroche "Paul Delaroche"), 1828

The Battle of Trocadero was one of the events that prompted U.S. President [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe") to proclaim what would become known as the [Monroe Doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monroe_Doctrine "Monroe Doctrine") on 2 December 1823, to safeguard the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas "Americas") against intervention by European powers.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Trocadero#cite_note-3)

The fall of Trocadero was commemorated in Paris, with the [Trocadéro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trocad%C3%A9ro,_Paris "Trocadéro, Paris"), where the city was expanding to the edges of the [Bois de Boulogne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bois_de_Boulogne "Bois de Boulogne"). [Louis-Antoine, Duke of Angoulême](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis-Antoine,_Duke_of_Angoul%C3%AAme "Louis-Antoine, Duke of Angoulême"), the victor of the battle, was offered the title "Prince of Trocadero" by the Spanish king, but he refused to accept it, partly in disgust at Ferdinand going back on his promises of clemency.

In _[Les Misérables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les\_Mis%C3%A9rables "Les Misérables")_, [Victor Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Hugo "Victor Hugo") devoted several paragraphs to the battle (Volume II, Book 2, chapter 3), in which he called the battle "a fine military action", but also said that "[t]he war of 1823 was an outrage on the generous Spanish nation, (..) at the same time, an outrage on the French Revolution."

El duque de Angulema en la batalla de Trocadero, por [Hippolyte Delaroche](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippolyte_Delaroche "Hippolyte Delaroche").

La **batalla del [Trocadero](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isla_del_Trocadero "Isla del Trocadero")** tuvo lugar el 31 de agosto de 1823. Fue un encuentro bélico que puso fin al [Trienio Liberal](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trienio_Liberal "Trienio Liberal") español (1820-1823) y restauró al [monarca absolutista](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarqu%C3%ADa_absoluta "Monarquía absoluta")[Fernando VII](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_VII "Fernando VII"), dando inicio a la «[Década Ominosa](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9cada_Ominosa "Década Ominosa")» (1823-1833). La intervención de tropas francesas llamadas los _[Cien Mil hijos de San Luis](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cien\_Mil\_hijos\_de\_San\_Luis "Cien Mil hijos de San Luis")_ hizo acabar el enfrentamiento a favor del bando tradicionalista que se enfrentaba a la revolución constitucional.

## Preludio

[[editar](http://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Batalla_del_Trocadero&action=edit&section=1 "Editar sección: Preludio")]

Las potencias europeas vigilaron durante tres años las luchas entre distintas facciones en España, cuando [Fernando VII](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_VII "Fernando VII") rechazó restaurar la [Constitución liberal de 1812](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituci%C3%B3n_de_1812 "Constitución de 1812") y tuvo que hacer frente a la revolución acaecida en el país desde 1820 a raíz de la sublevación del constitucionalista [Rafael de Riego](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_de_Riego "Rafael de Riego") al frente de tropas destinadas a aplacar las rebeliones hispanoamericanas. El rey tuvo que restaurar la derogada [Constitución de 1812](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituci%C3%B3n_de_1812 "Constitución de 1812"), pero hizo un llamamiento internacional al [Congreso de Verona](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congreso_de_Verona "Congreso de Verona"), que se encontraba reunido en el territorio de [Italia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italia "Italia") controlado por [Austria](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria") en octubre de 1822. Los ministros de las distintas monarquías europeas se alarmaron ante la captura de Fernando VII por los revolucionarios liberales opuestos al absolutismo y que amenazaba la estabilidad del resto de los regímenes absolutistas en [Europa](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa "Europa"), coaligadas en la [Santa Alianza](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Alianza "Santa Alianza"), creada para prevenir movimientos de ese tipo.

El Congreso de Verona, con la abstención puntual del [Reino Unido](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reino_Unido_de_Gran_Breta%C3%B1a_e_Irlanda "Reino Unido de Gran Bretaña e Irlanda"), autorizó a [Francia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restauraci%C3%B3n_Francesa "Restauración Francesa") a intervenir en el conflicto restaurando el trono de Fernando. El 7 de abril de 1823 _[Cien Mil hijos de San Luis](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cien\_Mil\_hijos\_de\_San\_Luis "Cien Mil hijos de San Luis")_, liderados por el [duque de Angulema](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duque_de_Angulema "Duque de Angulema"), hijo del futuro [Carlos X de Francia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_X_de_Francia "Carlos X de Francia"), cruzaron los [Pirineos](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirineos "Pirineos"), entrando en España. Fueron bien recibidos en el [País Vasco](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pa%C3%ADs_Vasco "País Vasco"), [Navarra](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navarra "Navarra") y en [Cataluña](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalu%C3%B1a "Cataluña"), avanzando entre las aclamaciones populares. Sin embargo, el duque tuvo que [asediar Pamplona](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asedio_de_Pamplona_(1823) "Asedio de Pamplona (1823)") y [San Sebastián](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Sebasti%C3%A1n "San Sebastián") (que capituló el 27 de septiembre[[2]](http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batalla_del_Trocadero#cite_note-2)) . El 23 de mayo de 1823 el gobierno liberal se trasladó de Madrid a [Sevilla](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevilla "Sevilla"), llevando consigo al rey Fernando VII en calidad de rehén. El comandante militar de Madrid capituló en secreto y huyó a Francia, y las guarniciones no pudieron liberar Madrid de los franceses, que instalaron al Duque del Infantado como [regente](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_de_Alc%C3%A1ntara_%C3%81lvarez_de_Toledo "Pedro de Alcántara Álvarez de Toledo") hasta la llegada del rey Fernando.

## La batalla

[[editar](http://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Batalla_del_Trocadero&action=edit&section=2 "Editar sección: La batalla")]

Las fuerzas francesas llegarían hasta [Cádiz](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1diz "Cádiz") en busca del rey y, con objeto de capturar la ciudad, asediaron la isla donde estaba el [fuerte del Trocadero](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuerte_de_San_Luis "Fuerte de San Luis") ([Puerto Real](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Real "Puerto Real")), que controlaba el acceso a aquella. El 31 de agosto de 1823 los franceses lanzarían un ataque sorpresa con [bayonetas](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayoneta "Bayoneta") atacando desde la costa aprovechando la marea baja y tomando el fuerte. Hubo 141 bajas francesas y entre 400 y 500 españolas, y más de 1000 prisioneros.[[3]](http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batalla_del_Trocadero#cite_note-3) El ataque fue tan súbito que no hubo siquiera opción de escapar.

El ejército francés tomó la fortificación construyendo nuevas baterías que apuntaban a Cádiz.[[4]](http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batalla_del_Trocadero#cite_note-4) La ciudad fue bombardeada durante tres semanas. El duque de Angulema tenía el control de la bahía, pero la única forma de entrar en la ciudad era por el único paso terrestre que tenía, a través de San Fernando por el [puente Zuazo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puente_Zuazo "Puente Zuazo"), que se encontraba fuertemente defendido. El duque se decidió a bombardear el [castillo de Sancti-Petri](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castillo_de_Sancti_Petri "Castillo de Sancti Petri") e intentar un desembarco en la punta del Boquerón, para continuar a pie hasta Cádiz. El día 20 de septiembre se abrió fuego contra el fuerte, que se rindió de inmediato, y el día 23 el chambelán de Fernando VII, el duque de Valmediana, se reunió con el duque para comunicarle que el rey estaba libre y se reuniría con él donde establecieran. Fernando embarcó en una barcaza que lo llevó de Cádiz a El Puerto de Santa María, donde se reunió con el duque.

La Ciudad de Cádiz se rendiría finalmente el 3 de octubre.[[5]](http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batalla_del_Trocadero#cite_note-5)

## Consecuencias de la batalla

[[editar](http://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Batalla_del_Trocadero&action=edit&section=3 "Editar sección: Consecuencias de la batalla")]

Renunciando a su compromiso de [amnistía](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnist%C3%ADa "Amnistía") con los revolucionarios, el rey ordenó represalias despiadadas mientras estuvieron las tropas francesas. En los siguientes años fueron ejecutadas 30.000 personas. El rey además abolió nuevamente la Constitución de 1812, dando paso a una década absolutista llamada [década ominosa](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9cada_ominosa "Década ominosa") por sus opositores de entonces y la mayor parte de los historiadores.

Para conmemorar la victoria, en París se dio el nombre de la isla y del fuerte a una [plaza](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_del_Trocadero "Plaza del Trocadero"). El [duque de Angulema](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duque_de_Angulema "Duque de Angulema") recibió el título de «[Príncipe del Trocadero](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%ADncipe_del_Trocadero?action=edit&redlink=1 "Príncipe del Trocadero (aún no redactado)")» y el escritor [François-René de Chateaubriand](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois-Ren%C3%A9_de_Chateaubriand "François-René de Chateaubriand") escribió en sus memorias:

> ¡Por aplastar a los españoles en un paso, por tener éxito donde Bonaparte fracasó, por triunfar en la misma tierra donde los ejércitos de aquel gran hombre sufrieron la adversidad, por hacer en seis meses lo que él no pudo hacer en siete años, esto es una gran maravilla!

El duque de Angulema en la batalla de Trocadero, por [Hippolyte Delaroche](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippolyte_Delaroche "Hippolyte Delaroche").

La **batalla del [Trocadero](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isla_del_Trocadero "Isla del Trocadero")** tuvo lugar el 31 de agosto de 1823. Fue un encuentro bélico que puso fin al [Trienio Liberal](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trienio_Liberal "Trienio Liberal") español (1820-1823) y restauró al [monarca absolutista](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarqu%C3%ADa_absoluta "Monarquía absoluta")[Fernando VII](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_VII "Fernando VII"), dando inicio a la «[Década Ominosa](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9cada_Ominosa "Década Ominosa")» (1823-1833). La intervención de tropas francesas llamadas los _[Cien Mil hijos de San Luis](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cien\_Mil\_hijos\_de\_San\_Luis "Cien Mil hijos de San Luis")_ hizo acabar el enfrentamiento a favor del bando tradicionalista que se enfrentaba a la revolución constitucional.

## Preludio

[[editar](http://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Batalla_del_Trocadero&action=edit&section=1 "Editar sección: Preludio")]

Las potencias europeas vigilaron durante tres años las luchas entre distintas facciones en España, cuando [Fernando VII](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_VII "Fernando VII") rechazó restaurar la [Constitución liberal de 1812](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituci%C3%B3n_de_1812 "Constitución de 1812") y tuvo que hacer frente a la revolución acaecida en el país desde 1820 a raíz de la sublevación del constitucionalista [Rafael de Riego](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_de_Riego "Rafael de Riego") al frente de tropas destinadas a aplacar las rebeliones hispanoamericanas. El rey tuvo que restaurar la derogada [Constitución de 1812](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituci%C3%B3n_de_1812 "Constitución de 1812"), pero hizo un llamamiento internacional al [Congreso de Verona](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congreso_de_Verona "Congreso de Verona"), que se encontraba reunido en el territorio de [Italia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italia "Italia") controlado por [Austria](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria") en octubre de 1822. Los ministros de las distintas monarquías europeas se alarmaron ante la captura de Fernando VII por los revolucionarios liberales opuestos al absolutismo y que amenazaba la estabilidad del resto de los regímenes absolutistas en [Europa](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa "Europa"), coaligadas en la [Santa Alianza](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Alianza "Santa Alianza"), creada para prevenir movimientos de ese tipo.

El Congreso de Verona, con la abstención puntual del [Reino Unido](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reino_Unido_de_Gran_Breta%C3%B1a_e_Irlanda "Reino Unido de Gran Bretaña e Irlanda"), autorizó a [Francia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restauraci%C3%B3n_Francesa "Restauración Francesa") a intervenir en el conflicto restaurando el trono de Fernando. El 7 de abril de 1823 _[Cien Mil hijos de San Luis](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cien\_Mil\_hijos\_de\_San\_Luis "Cien Mil hijos de San Luis")_, liderados por el [duque de Angulema](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duque_de_Angulema "Duque de Angulema"), hijo del futuro [Carlos X de Francia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_X_de_Francia "Carlos X de Francia"), cruzaron los [Pirineos](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirineos "Pirineos"), entrando en España. Fueron bien recibidos en el [País Vasco](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pa%C3%ADs_Vasco "País Vasco"), [Navarra](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navarra "Navarra") y en [Cataluña](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalu%C3%B1a "Cataluña"), avanzando entre las aclamaciones populares. Sin embargo, el duque tuvo que [asediar Pamplona](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asedio_de_Pamplona_(1823) "Asedio de Pamplona (1823)") y [San Sebastián](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Sebasti%C3%A1n "San Sebastián") (que capituló el 27 de septiembre[[2]](http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batalla_del_Trocadero#cite_note-2)) . El 23 de mayo de 1823 el gobierno liberal se trasladó de Madrid a [Sevilla](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevilla "Sevilla"), llevando consigo al rey Fernando VII en calidad de rehén. El comandante militar de Madrid capituló en secreto y huyó a Francia, y las guarniciones no pudieron liberar Madrid de los franceses, que instalaron al Duque del Infantado como [regente](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_de_Alc%C3%A1ntara_%C3%81lvarez_de_Toledo "Pedro de Alcántara Álvarez de Toledo") hasta la llegada del rey Fernando.

## La batalla

[[editar](http://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Batalla_del_Trocadero&action=edit&section=2 "Editar sección: La batalla")]

Las fuerzas francesas llegarían hasta [Cádiz](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1diz "Cádiz") en busca del rey y, con objeto de capturar la ciudad, asediaron la isla donde estaba el [fuerte del Trocadero](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuerte_de_San_Luis "Fuerte de San Luis") ([Puerto Real](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Real "Puerto Real")), que controlaba el acceso a aquella. El 31 de agosto de 1823 los franceses lanzarían un ataque sorpresa con [bayonetas](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayoneta "Bayoneta") atacando desde la costa aprovechando la marea baja y tomando el fuerte. Hubo 141 bajas francesas y entre 400 y 500 españolas, y más de 1000 prisioneros.[[3]](http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batalla_del_Trocadero#cite_note-3) El ataque fue tan súbito que no hubo siquiera opción de escapar.

El ejército francés tomó la fortificación construyendo nuevas baterías que apuntaban a Cádiz.[[4]](http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batalla_del_Trocadero#cite_note-4) La ciudad fue bombardeada durante tres semanas. El duque de Angulema tenía el control de la bahía, pero la única forma de entrar en la ciudad era por el único paso terrestre que tenía, a través de San Fernando por el [puente Zuazo](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puente_Zuazo "Puente Zuazo"), que se encontraba fuertemente defendido. El duque se decidió a bombardear el [castillo de Sancti-Petri](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castillo_de_Sancti_Petri "Castillo de Sancti Petri") e intentar un desembarco en la punta del Boquerón, para continuar a pie hasta Cádiz. El día 20 de septiembre se abrió fuego contra el fuerte, que se rindió de inmediato, y el día 23 el chambelán de Fernando VII, el duque de Valmediana, se reunió con el duque para comunicarle que el rey estaba libre y se reuniría con él donde establecieran. Fernando embarcó en una barcaza que lo llevó de Cádiz a El Puerto de Santa María, donde se reunió con el duque.

La Ciudad de Cádiz se rendiría finalmente el 3 de octubre.[[5]](http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batalla_del_Trocadero#cite_note-5)

## Consecuencias de la batalla

[[editar](http://es.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Batalla_del_Trocadero&action=edit&section=3 "Editar sección: Consecuencias de la batalla")]

Renunciando a su compromiso de [amnistía](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnist%C3%ADa "Amnistía") con los revolucionarios, el rey ordenó represalias despiadadas mientras estuvieron las tropas francesas. En los siguientes años fueron ejecutadas 30.000 personas. El rey además abolió nuevamente la Constitución de 1812, dando paso a una década absolutista llamada [década ominosa](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9cada_ominosa "Década ominosa") por sus opositores de entonces y la mayor parte de los historiadores.

Para conmemorar la victoria, en París se dio el nombre de la isla y del fuerte a una [plaza](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_del_Trocadero "Plaza del Trocadero"). El [duque de Angulema](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duque_de_Angulema "Duque de Angulema") recibió el título de «[Príncipe del Trocadero](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%ADncipe_del_Trocadero?action=edit&redlink=1 "Príncipe del Trocadero (aún no redactado)")» y el escritor [François-René de Chateaubriand](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois-Ren%C3%A9_de_Chateaubriand "François-René de Chateaubriand") escribió en sus memorias:

> ¡Por aplastar a los españoles en un paso, por tener éxito donde Bonaparte fracasó, por triunfar en la misma tierra donde los ejércitos de aquel gran hombre sufrieron la adversidad, por hacer en seis meses lo que él no pudo hacer en siete años, esto es una gran maravilla!
